source.title: An Embarrassingly Simple Defense Against LLM Abliteration Attacks
source.authors: H. Shairah; Hasan Abed Al Kader Hammoud; Bernard Ghanem; G. Turkiyyah

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether extended-refusal fine-tuning improves safety robustness, using abliteration, benign fine-tuning, jailbreak evaluations, and a prompt-injection example. It does not reproduce the cited studies’ token-position KL measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results for abliteration, benign fine-tuning, jailbreak benchmarks, refusal-component ablations, an injected-opening example, and hidden-state distances. Its discussion of token-position concentration and harmful fine-tuning is attributed to prior work; no per-token KL result is reported here.
record.test_reason: The paper trains models on extended refusals (explanation first, refusal later), a deepening defense (V7). It measures its robustness with its own numbers: abliteration, six jailbreak benchmarks, benign fine-tuning and a prompt-injection example. Its control models also give its own results on benign fine-tuning erosion (V2), single-direction removal of refusal (V5) and an injected compliant opening (V4). It reports no per-token KL and no harmful fine-tuning.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that extended-refusal fine-tuning (explanation, then refusal, then justification) disperses the refusal signal, so refusal stays above 90% under abliteration against below 20% for standard models. They say it generalizes to jailbreaks, prompt injection and benign fine-tuning drift, and that 'the form of safety expression is itself a mechanism of safety'. They claim general performance is preserved before abliteration. They acknowledge utility and coherence loss after abliteration, a moderate decline under benign fine-tuning, verbosity, and untested generality above 7B.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains models on a 10,000-example mixture of extended harmful-request refusals and benign Alpaca-GPT4-en instructions, then evaluates resistance to abliteration and other attacks. It does not reproduce the cited studies’ fine-tuning or token-wise KL recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model, attack benchmark, training-data component, benign fine-tuning progress, and safety judge. The authors report that Qwen2.5-1.5B extended-refusal directions at token positions −2 and −5 do not produce coherent models, but this is not a refusal-rate result.

fits_no_version.finding: Abliteration shrinks the harmful-vs-benign final-hidden-state centroid distance much less in extended-refusal models (7.7–13.7 points) than in standard models (28.7–33.9 points).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extended-refusal training preserves the representational separation of harmful and benign prompts under direction removal.

record.code_released: The authors say the dataset and models will be made publicly available; no URL is stated.
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the cited results. The benign fine-tuning trajectory is presented as a figure without exact stepwise refusal values in the text. The prompt-injection result is a single example, not a rate. The authors note coherence and utility costs after abliteration, and say generalization to larger models remains uncertain.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results relevant to the versions were left out.

untested.parts: No aligned-vs-base per-token KL or per-position analysis.
Only one prefill-style injection example. No adversarial suffixes, decoding attacks or prefilling rates.
Only a single residual direction (rank-one projection) is tested. No search for a minimal set of weights or ranks.
The paper hypothesises that brief, formulaic refusals cause the concentration but does not test standard training data or objectives.
Does not measure whether safety is actually spread across response token positions. No prefilling-depth attack rates, no harmful fine-tuning attack, and no models above 7B.
Only one model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) and one dataset (Dolly 15K).

missing.what: Utility and coherence for each model before and after abliteration. Examples: Llama-extended coherence 89.1 and MMLU 41.8 after abliteration (46.4 before); Qwen1.5B-extended perplexity 26.7→49.5; MMLU cost of extended-refusal training alone 0.5–1.3. Needed for any cost-of-deepening comparison.
Refusal of extended-refusal models before abliteration is 100 for all three, against 93.1/93.8 for the standard Qwen models, so the training itself raises refusal.
Refusal and MMLU after abliterating every candidate layer×position direction. Qwen1.5B-extended directions at positions −2 and −5 yield no coherent model.
Standard-model jailbreak success rates, e.g. TrustLLM 39.0 and WildJailbreak 93.8 for Qwen2.5-3B. The prompt-injection-style attacks could be linked to V4 as standard-model baselines.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The deepening here is mainly framed against single-direction abliteration, not token-position depth; the token-depth link rests only on the injection example and the benign fine-tuning curve, and no per-position measurement is made. The paper's 'base' means the instruct model without extended-refusal training. No uncertainty is reported; small Llama jailbreak differences may be noise. The abliteration direction for the extended models is chosen under a coherence filter of at least 70%, so stronger, incoherence-causing directions are excluded by design. V6 is only hypothesised, with the refusal-only ablation as indirect evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful examples to measure whether they cause harmful compliance.
Tests benign fine-tuning on Databricks Dolly 15K for Qwen2.5-3B and its extended-refusal variant; does not test other models or benign datasets.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or comparison across response positions.
Shows one prompt-injection example with a supplied opening; does not separately test adversarial suffixes or decoding changes, or estimate rates for these attacks.
Does not identify a small set of weights or ranks carrying safety behaviour.

Does not directly test whether the data or objective used in conventional safety training causes shallow alignment. Component ablations examine the paper’s alternative training data, not the cause of shallowness in standard training.

Tests extended-refusal training against abliteration, selected jailbreak evaluations, and benign fine-tuning. It does not directly measure whether safety is spread across response-token positions or test persistence across other training methods and settings.
